parole.significato: the flower of the red poppy (Papaver rhoeas)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Andalusian Arabic حَبَّبَوْر (ḥabbabawr).
Borrowed from Andalusian Arabic صاحب الزاد (ṣāḥib az-zād, “owner of the provisions”). Or, from haba (“broad bean”), one of the provisions first sold at this store.
From a- + bancal (“terrace, plot of land”) + -ar. Bancal is possibly from Andalusian Arabic منقالة (manqála), or from banco (“bench (for rowers)”).

parole.significato: a member of a powerful faction, native to the Emirate of Granada, and rivals of the zegríes.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Andalusian Arabic بَنُو السَّرَّاج (banū as-sarrāj, literally “sons of the saddler”).
Inherited from Old Spanish [Term?], from Andalusian Arabic, from Arabic الزَّبُّوج (az-zabbūj).
Borrowed from Andalusian Arabic السَمِيد (as-samī́d), from Arabic سَمِيذ (samīḏ).

parole.significato: azarole, the fruit of the acerolo (Crataegus azarolus)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Andalusian Arabic الزَعْرُورَة (az-zaʕrúra), from Classical Arabic زُعْرُورَة (zuʕrūra).

parole.significato: barnacle, twitch, a kind of pincers or vise to fix the mouth of a horse or similar animals to yield the opportunity of…
parole.testo: From earlier aciar, from Andalusian Arabic الزِيَار (az-ziyār), from Arabic زِيَار (ziyār).
Borrowed from Andalusian Arabic السِّقَاط (as-siqáṭ). Compare Portuguese acicate.
Borrowed from Andalusian Arabic الصِرَاط (aṣ-ṣiráṭ), from Arabic صِرَاط (ṣirāṭ), from Classical Syriac ܐܣܛܪܛ (ˀesṭrāṭ), from Latin strāta. Doublet of estrada.

parole.significato: adarme, Spanish dram (a traditional unit of mass equivalent to about 1.8 g)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Andalusian Arabic الدرهم (ad-dárham), from Arabic دِرْهَم (dirham, “dirham”), from Middle Persian 𐭦𐭥𐭦𐭭 (drahm), from Ancient Greek δραχμή (drakhmḗ, “drachma”). Doublet of dracma and dírham.
Inherited from Old Spanish adarve, adarbe, from Andalusian Arabic الدَّرْب (ad-dárb), from Arabic دَرْب (darb, “path, pass, way”).
Borrowed from Andalusian Arabic, from Arabic الذِّئْب (aḏ-ḏiʔb).

From Andalusian Arabic الظُّوْبْ (aḍ-ḍób), from Arabic اَلطُّوب (aṭ-ṭūb), from Sahidic Coptic ⲧⲱⲃⲉ (tōbe, “brick”), from Demotic Egyptian ⁠⁠ (tb, “brick”), from Egyptian Db-b-t:O39 (ḏbt, “brick, block, ingot”).
Borrowed from Andalusian Arabic الدُّكَّان (ad-dukkán, ad-dukkín), from Arabic دُكَّان (dukkān).

Inherited from Old Spanish [Term?], from Andalusian Arabic *الدوان (ad-duwān, “the administrative office”), a variant of الديوان (ad-dīwān), from Arabic دِيوَان (dīwān, “administrative office”), from Persian دیوان (dêvân), ultimately from Sumerian 𒁾 (dub). Cognates include Portuguese aduana and (wit
Borrowed from Andalusian Arabic الدَرْمَكَ (ad-dármaka), from Arabic دَرْمَك (darmak).
Inherited from Old Spanish axeb, axep, from Andalusian Arabic اَلشَّبّ (aš-šabb), from Arabic شَبّ (šabb).
Borrowed from Andalusian Arabic اشترية (aš-šaṭríyya), from Latin satureia.
Inherited from Old Spanish axedrez, borrowed from Arabic شِطْرَنْج (šiṭranj) via Andalusian Arabic, from Middle Persian 𐭰𐭠𐭲𐭫𐭠𐭭𐭢 (cʾtlʾng /⁠čatrang⁠/), from Sanskrit चतुरङ्ग (caturaṅga).
Borrowed from Andalusian Arabic الشَّنُوز (aš-šanūz), Standard شُونِيز (šūnīz).
From Andalusian Arabic الشَّمِيس (aš-šamís).

Inherited from Old Spanish ajonjolí, aljonjolí, from an ambiguous Andalusian Arabic form, of raised final vowel from Arabic جُلْجُلَان (juljulān, “sesame seed”), or of clipped ending, جُلْجُل (juljul) + -í (nisba), as the descendants of the pomegranate cultivar سَفَرِيّ (safariyy), or rather + -ín (
From Andalusian Arabic الشُّرْكَة (aš-šúrka), from Arabic شِرَاك (širāk).
From Old Spanish axuar, borrowed from Andalusian Arabic الشِوَار (aš-šiwár), from Arabic شَوَار (šawār), شِوَار (šiwār).
Inherited from Old Spanish alacran, from Andalusian Arabic عَقْرَب (ʕaqráb), from Arabic عَقْرَب (ʕaqrab, “scorpion”).

parole.significato: a sweet paste of almonds, nuts and bread crumbs mixed with spices and honey
parole.testo: From Andalusian Arabic الحَشُو (al-ḥašú), from Arabic حَشْو (ḥašw, “stuffing, filling”).
From Andalusian Arabic عَلَم (ʕalam).
Borrowed from Andalusian Arabic, from Arabic عَرْض (ʕarḍ).

Borrowed from Andalusian Arabic أَرْغِيس (ʔarḡīs, “barberry”), a borrowing from Berber where arḡīs has been the bark of the root of barberry – azarġīnt the plant –, still present in the same form in Moroccan Arabic and Berber dialects.
From Andalusian Arabic العَرِيف (al-ʕaríf), from Arabic عَرِيف (ʕarīf, “expert”).
From Andalusian Arabic اَلْعَصْفُر (al-ʕaṣfúr), from Arabic اَلْعُصْفُر (al-ʕuṣfur, “safflower”).
From Andalusian Arabic الأصهاب (al-ʔaṣháb), from Arabic أَصْهَب (ʔaṣhab, “reddish, reddish-brown”).
Borrowed from Andalusian Arabic صَحْب الوَصِيَّة (çaḥb al-uacéah, literally “companion of the will”); see Arabic صَحْب (ṣaḥb), وَصِيَّة (waṣiyya).

parole.significato: breba, an early Ficus carica fig
parole.testo: From Andalusian Arabic اَلْبَاكُورَة (al-bācórah), from classical Arabic باكورة (bākūrah, “early fruits”).
From Andalusian Arabic الْبَرْدِي (al-bardiyy), from Arabic بَرْدِيّ (bardiyy).

Borrowed from Andalusian Arabic, from Arabic بَرْقُوق (barqūq), borrowed from Classical Syriac ܒܰܪܩܽܘܩܳܐ (barqūqā), from Byzantine Greek βερικοκκῐ́ᾱ (berikokkĭ́ā, “apricot tree”), from Ancient Greek βερίκοκκον (beríkokkon) + -ία (-ía). Doublet of precoz.
Borrowed from Andalusian Arabic البياض (al-bayáḍ), from Classical Arabic بَيَاض (bayāḍ, “whiteness, white lead”).
From Andalusian Arabic البِرْكَة (al-birka), from Arabic بِرْكَة (birka, “pond”). Compare Portuguese alverca.
From Andalusian Arabic البُرُوز (al-burúz), from Arabic بُرُوز (burūz).
Borrowed from Andalusian Arabic البُشْرَى (al-búšra), from Arabic بُشْرَى (bušrā, “good news”).
From Andalusian Arabic اَلْبَطِّيخَة (al-baṭṭīḵa, “watermelon”), from Arabic بَطِّيخَة (baṭṭīḵa, “watermelon”).
From Andalusian Arabic البوري (al-búri), from Arabic بُورِيّ (būriyy), named from a city in Egypt.

From Andalusian Arabic البُنْدُقَة (al-bunduqa, “the hazelnut”), from Arabic بُنْدُق (bunduq, “hazelnut, pebble, bullet”), from Middle Persian pndk' (pondik, “hazelnut”), from Ancient Greek Ποντικὸν κάρυον (Pontikòn káruon, “Pontic nut”). Compare Ladino albondiga and Portuguese almôndega.
Borrowed from Andalusian Arabic القبالة (al-qabála), from Arabic قبالة (qabāla).

Inherited from Old Spanish alcarchofa, from Andalusian Arabic الخرشوفة (al-ḵaršúfa), from Arabic الخُرْشُوف (al-ḵuršūf, “artichoke”). Compare Portuguese alcachofra and Catalan carxofa. Related to English artichoke.
From Andalusian Arabic القَوَّاد (al-qawwád), from Arabic قَوَّاد (qawwād, “pimp”). Cognate with Portuguese alcaguete.

parole.significato: to act as a go-between, to play Cupid
parole.testo: From alcahuete + -ar, from Andalusian Arabic القواد (al-qawwád), from Arabic قَوَّاد (qawwād).

parole.significato: A public marketplace where silk merchants would expose their merchandise in order to be charged with the duties they ow…
parole.testo: From Andalusian Arabic القَيْصَرِيَّة (alqayṣaríyya), from Arabic اَلـ (al-, “the”) + قَيْصَر (qayṣar, “Caesar; emperor”) + ـِيّة (-iyya, noun-forming relational suffix), after the fact that such places were built by imperial decree. Cognate with Portuguese alcaçaria.
Derived from Arabic كَنْز (kanz), via Andalusian Arabic. Cognate with Portuguese alcanzia.
Borrowed from Andalusian Arabic, from Arabic قَنْدُورَة (qandūra).
Borrowed from Andalusian Arabic, from Arabic كَافُور (kāfūr).

parole.significato: plateau, especially one bare of vegetation
parole.testo: From the region of La Alcarria in central Spain, which is characterised by this sort of topography, from Andalusian Arabic اَلْقَرِيَّة (al-qaríyya), from Arabic اَلْقَرْيَة (al-qarya, “the village”). Doublet of alquería.
From Andalusian Arabic الْقَبْسِيل (al-qabsīl), from a Medieval Latin form *capicella for capitia, from Latin caput (“head”). Doublet of jefe and cabo.

parole.significato: shrike (any of various passerine birds of the family Laniidae which are known for their habit of catching other birds a…
parole.testo: From Andalusian Arabic القَبْطُون (*al-qabṭún), from Arabic قُبْطان (qubṭān).
From Andalusian Arabic الخَيَاطَة, from Latin cāia.
Inherited from Old Spanish alcofol, alcofor, alcohol (c. 1200), from Andalusian Arabic اَلْكُحُول (al-kuḥū́l), from Arabic اَلْكُحْل (al-kuḥl, “kohl”).
From Andalusian Arabic آلقُلّ (alqúll), from Latin collis.
From Andalusian Arabic القُطَان (al-quṭan), from Arabic قَطَام (qaṭām).
From Andalusian Arabic *الكنیه (al-kúnya), from Arabic كُنْيَة (kunya, “kunya”).
From Andalusian Arabic الكُوزَة (al-kúza), from Arabic كُوزَة (kūza).

parole.significato: mortise, rabbet (on the keel or stem)
parole.testo: From Andalusian Arabic الإِفْرِيز (al-ʔifríz), from Arabic إِفْرِيز (ʔifrīz), apocope of Classical Syriac ܦܪܝܙܘܡܐ (pərīzōmāʾ), from Ancient Greek περίζωμα (perízōma, “girdle”).

parole.significato: larch tree (trees of the genus Larix)
parole.testo: From Andalusian Arabic اَلْأَرْز (al-ʔarz), from Classical Arabic أَرْز (ʔarz, “cedar”).
Borrowed from Andalusian Arabic الإِطْرِيَّة (al-ʔitriyya), from Arabic الْإِطْرِيَة (al-ʔiṭriya), from Aramaic אִטְרִיתָא (ʾiṭrīṯā), from Ancient Greek ἴτριον (ítrion). Compare Portuguese aletria.

From Andalusian Arabic العَيْب (al-ʕáyb), from Arabic عَيْب (ʕayb, “fault, defect”). Originally only used as a noun, it started being used as an adjective in the 16th century, possibly guided by leve or by phrases like le mató a leve.
From Andalusian Arabic الآيَة (al-ʔáya), from Arabic آيَة (ʔāya).
From Andalusian Arabic الهَدِيَّة (al-hadíyya), from Arabic هَدِيَّة (hadiyya, “donation, offering”).
Inherited from Old Spanish alfaguara, from Andalusian Arabic اَلْفَوَّارَة (al-fawwāra), from Arabic فَوَّارَة (fawwāra, “spring, fountain”).

parole.significato: A popular confection in Andalusia usually made with honey, almonds, nuts, and spices such as clove and coriander.
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Spanish alfaxor, beginning as a more jammy food from Andalusian Arabic الْفَشُور (al-fašūr, “nectar, juice”), from Arabic أَفْشُرَج (ʔafšuraj, “juice”). Somewhere surely mixed up with alfaxú, alajú from حَشْو (ḥašw, “filling”).

parole.significato: cutlass (sword of European origin with a straight or slightly curved blade)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Andalusian Arabic, from Arabic خَنْجَر (ḵanjar)
From Andalusian Arabic, from Arabic الحَاجِز (al-ḥājiz).
From Andalusian Arabic الفَقِيه (al-faqíh), from Arabic الفَقِيه (al-faqīh, “the theologian”).
From Andalusian Arabic الْفَخَّار (al-faḵḵār), from Arabic فَخَّار (faḵḵār, “pottery”), from Aramaic פחרא / ܦܚܪܐ (paḵḵārā), from Akkadian 𒁃 (BAḪAR₂ /⁠paḫāru⁠/).
From alfar + -ero, from Andalusian Arabic الْفَخَّار (al-faḵḵār), from Arabic فَخَّار (faḵḵār, “pottery”), from Aramaic פחרא / ܦܚܪܐ (paḵḵārā), from Akkadian 𒁃 (BAḪAR₂ /⁠paḫāru⁠/).
From Andalusian Arabic الفَالِجِيَّة (al-falijíyya), from Arabic فَالِج (fālij, “stroke”), from Ancient Greek ἀποπληξία (apoplēxía, “apoplexy”).

parole.significato: pin (a needle without an eye used for fastening)
parole.testo: From the older alfilel, from Andalusian Arabic اَلْخِلَال (al-ḵilál), from Classical Arabic خِلَال (ḵilāl, “pin, peg”).
From Andalusian Arabic الحِيْز (alḥíz), from Arabic الحَيِّز (al-ḥayyiz).
Borrowed from Andalusian Arabic الهُرِي (al-hurī), from Classical هُرْي (hury), هُرِيّ (huriyy).
Derived from Andalusian Arabic الحنبل (al-ḥánbal). Doublet of arambel and alhamar.
From Andalusian Arabic الخُرْج (al-ḵurj), from Arabic خُرْج (ḵurj, “saddlebag”).
From Andalusian Arabic الحُزَّة (al-ḥúzza), from Arabic الحُغْزَة (al-ḥuḡza). Cognate with Asturian llorza.

parole.significato: during the Middle Ages, the rural territory belonging to a corresponding town
parole.testo: From Andalusian Arabic الحَوْز (al-ḥáwz), from Arabic حَوْز (ḥawz, literally “possession”), formed as a verbal noun of حَازَ (ḥāza).
From Andalusian Arabic الحيزا (al-ḥéyza), from Arabic حِيَازَة (ḥiyāza, “tenure”), from Arabic حَيِّز (ḥayyiz, “space”).
Borrowed from Arabic فَارِس (fāris), via Andalusian Arabic الْفَارِس (al-fāris).
From Andalusian Arabic الفستق (al-fústaq), from Arabic فُسْتَق (fustaq, “pistachio”). Compare Catalan festuc.
From Andalusian Arabic الغَالِيَة (al-ḡáliya), from Arabic غَالِيَّة (ḡāliyya).
Borrowed from Andalusian Arabic اَلْغَار (al-ḡár), from Arabic اَلْغَار (al-ḡār, “grotto”).
Borrowed from Andalusian Arabic الخَرُّوبَة (al-ḵarrū́ba), from Arabic خَرُّوبَة (ḵarrūba).
From Andalusian Arabic الغَزَارَة (al-ḡazára), from Arabic الغَزَارَة (al-ḡazāra, “abundance”).
From Andalusian Arabic, from Arabic الحَاجَة (al-ḥāja, “necessary thing; valuable thing”); or الحِلْيَة (al-ḥilya, “ornament”).
From Andalusian Arabic الحنبل (al-ḥánbal), from Arabic حَنْبَل (ḥanbal, “ceremonial tapestry”). Doublet of alfombra and arambel.
From Andalusian Arabic الحَرَٰكَة (al-ḥaráka), from Arabic حَرَكَة (ḥaraka). Cognate with Asturian ḥarca.
From Andalusian Arabic الْحُلْبَة (al-ḥúlba), from Arabic حُلْبَة (ḥulba). Compare Portuguese alforba.
Borrowed from Andalusian Arabic الْخُزَامَى (al-ḵuzáma), from Arabic الْخُزَامَى (al-ḵuzāmā).
From Andalusian Arabic الفُنْدَق (al-fúndaq), from Arabic فُنْدُق (funduq, “inn, hotel”), from Ancient Greek πανδοκεῖον (pandokeîon, “inn”). Cognate to Catalan alfòndec and Portuguese alfândega.
From Andalusian Arabic القطع (al-qáṭaʕ), from Arabic قَطْع (qaṭʕ).

parole.significato: a meal as part of a business deal
parole.testo: From Andalusian Arabic الإِحَالَة (al-ʕiḥála), from Arabic إِحَالَة (ʔiḥāla, “transfer”).
From Andalusian Arabic الجمع (al-jámaʕ), from Arabic جَمْع (jamʕ).
From Andalusian Arabic اَلْجُبّ (al-júbb), from Classical Arabic جُبّ (jubb, “cistern, well”). Cognate with Galician alxibe and Catalan aljub. Compare Sicilian gebbia.
Borrowed from Andalusian Arabic الجَّفِّفَة, from ال (al-) + جَفِّفَة (jaffifa, “a dry sponge used as floorcloth”).
Inherited from Old Spanish [Term?], from Andalusian Arabic جبة (al-gubba), from Arabic جُبَّة (jubba). Doublet of chupa. Cognate with Portuguese aljuba.
From Andalusian Arabic اللَوْزَة (al-lawza), from Arabic لَوْزَة (lawza, “almond”).
Borrowed from Andalusian Arabic المَخْزَن (al-maḵzán, “the warehouse”), from Arabic مَخْزَن (maḵzan). Cognate with Portuguese armazém. Doublet of magacín.
From Andalusian Arabic المضربة (almaḍrába).
Borrowed from Andalusian Arabic المَعْدِيَّة (al-maʕdiyya).
From earlier almagra, from Andalusian Arabic المغرة (al-máḡra), from Arabic الْمَغْرَة (al-maḡra), الْمُغْرَة (al-muḡra, “red clay or earth”).
Borrowed from Andalusian Arabic الْمَنَاخ (al-manāḵ, “almanac, calendar”), from Arabic الْمُنَاخ (al-munāḵ, “climate”).
From Andalusian Arabic المَحْلَج (*al-maḥláj), from Arabic مَحْلَج (maḥlaj).
From Andalusian Arabic المَعْصَرَة (al-maʕṣára), from Arabic مَعْصَرَة (maʕṣara, “press”). Cognate of Catalan almàssera.
From Andalusian Arabic المَنَارَة (al-manára), from Arabic مَنَارَة (manāra).
From Andalusian Arabic المَنْهَر (al-manhár), from Arabic مَنْهَر (manhar).
Borrowed from Andalusian Arabic الميس (al-méys), from Arabic مَيْس (mays, “a kind of tree”).
From Andalusian Arabic الميس (al-méys), from Arabic مَيْس (mays, “a kind of tree”).
Borrowed from Andalusian Arabic المسك (al-mísk), from Arabic مِسْك (misk), from Persian مشک (mošk), from Sanskrit मुष्क (muṣka, “testicle, scrotum”).

According to Corominas and Pascual, probably from Andalusian Arabic al-mukáffir, from Arabic مُكَفِّر (mukaffir), active participle of Arabic كَفَّرَ (kaffara, “to cover, hide”), ultimately from the root ك ف ر (k f r). Less likely, RAE proposes Andalusian Arabic *abu káff, from Arabic أَبُو كف (“the

parole.significato: a type of matress made of a sack stuffed with straw or corn leaves
parole.testo: Borrowed from Andalusian Arabic الْمُصَلَّى (al-muṣallā), from Arabic مصلى (muṣallan, “a place of prayer”). Doublet of almozala.
Inherited from Old Spanish almofalla, from Andalusian Arabic, from Arabic اَلْمَحَلَّة (al-maḥalla, “encampment”), from حَلَّ (ḥalla, “to dismount”).
From Andalusian Arabic المُغَاوِر (al-muḡā́wir), from Arabic مُغَاوِر (muḡāwir).

parole.significato: pillow (soft cushion used to support the head)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Andalusian Arabic مُخَدَّة (muḵadda), from Arabic مِخَدَّة (miḵadda, “pillow”). Cognate with Asturian almuhada (“pillow”), Aragonese almada (“pillow”), Galician and Portuguese almofada (“pillow, cushion”), Leonese almugada, olmada (“pillow”).
From Andalusian Arabic *المُوَحَّد (*al-muwaḥḥád), from Arabic مُوَحِّد (muwaḥḥid).
Borrowed from Andalusian Arabic, from Arabic مِحَسَّة (miḥassa).

parole.significato: a Colombian bread made with cheese and flour
parole.testo: From Andalusian Arabic المُجَٰبَّنَة (al-mujábbana, “made of cheese”), from Arabic جُبْن (jubn, “cheese”).
From Andalusian Arabic المُنَادَة (al-munáda), from Arabic مُنَادَاة (munādāh). Cognate with Galician almoeda and Portuguese almoeda.
Borrowed from Andalusian Arabic الْمَرْدَدُّوش (al-mardadúš), from Arabic مَرْدَقُوش (mardaqūš).
Borrowed from Andalusian Arabic [Term?], from Arabic مُرَابِط (murābiṭ).
Borrowed from Andalusian Arabic الْمُصَلَّى (al-muṣallā), from Arabic مصلى (muṣallan, “a place of prayer”). Doublet of almocela.

parole.significato: synonym of celemín (a traditional unit of dry measure equivalent to about 4.6 liters)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Andalusian Arabic المُدّ (al-mudd), from Arabic مُدّ (mudd), probably via Aramaic 𐡬𐡣𐡩𐡠 (mdyʾ) and מוֹדְיָא (moḏyā) or Classical Syriac ܡܘܿܕܝܳܐ (moḏyā) from Akkadian 𒉘𒈨𒌍 (/⁠maddattu, middattu⁠/, “kind of vessel, unit of volume”). Cognate with Ancient Greek μόδιος (módios) and Latin modi
Borrowed from Andalusian Arabic, from Arabic مَسْقًى (masqan).

parole.significato: a yellowy resin extracted from Pistacia lentiscus (mastic tree), mastic
parole.testo: Borrowed from Andalusian Arabic, from Arabic مُصْطَكَى (muṣṭakā, “mastic”).

From Andalusian Arabic الْمَاطَنَة (al-māṭana, “sledgehammer”), of unclear origin, speculated from Ancient Greek πατάνη (patánē, “a flat dish”) reanalyzed as a tool noun which has also been borrowed as بَطَانَة (baṭāna), پَطَانَة (paṭāna, “dishware or other large thing of little value”), because of
From Andalusian Arabic *اَلْمَرْتَعَة (*al-mártaʕa), from Arabic مَرْتَع (martaʕ, “pasture”), from رِتَاع (ritāʕ, “grazing”).
From Andalusian Arabic البَرْغَات (al-barḡāt), plural of بَرْغَة (barḡa). Ultimately from the same source as abarca (“sandal”), probably Basque abarka.
Borrowed from Andalusian Arabic البِشْط (al-bišṭ), from Latin pistum.
From Andalusian Arabic اَلْقَرِيَّة (al-qaríyya), from Arabic اَلْقَرْيَة (al-qarya, “the village”). Doublet of alcarria.
From Andalusian Arabic القِبْلَة (al-qíbla), from Arabic قِبْلَة (qibla).

parole.significato: rent (a payment made in exchange for something borrowed, and its amount)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Arabic كِرَاءْ (kirāʔ), via Andalusian Arabic الكِرِاءْ.

Inherited from Old Spanish alquimia, from Andalusian Arabic اَلْكِيمْيَا (al-kímya) and Medieval Latin alchemia, from Arabic اَلْكِيمِيَاء (al-kīmiyāʔ), from Ancient Greek χυμείᾱ (khumeíā, “art of alloying metals”), from χύμα (khúma, “ingot, bar”).
From alcatara, from Andalusian Arabic القطارة (al-qaṭṭára), from Arabic قَطَّارَة (qaṭṭāra).
From Andalusian Arabic اَلْقِطْرَان (al-qiṭrán), from Arabic قِطْرَان (qiṭrān, “tar”). Compare Portuguese alcatrão.

parole.significato: lupin (any member of the genus Lupinus in the family Fabaceae)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Andalusian Arabic التَرْمُوس (at-tarmús), from Arabic تُرْمُس (turmus, “lupin”), via Aramaic from Akkadian 𒋻𒄷 (TAR.MUŠ₈ /⁠tarmuš⁠/), from Sumerian 𒋻𒄷 (TAR.MUŠ₈ /⁠tarmuš⁠/).
Borrowed from Andalusian Arabic اللُوبِيَاء (al-lúbiaʔ), from Arabic لُوبِيَاء (lūbīyāʔ), from Persian لوبیا (lubiyâ).
From Andalusian Arabic النَّافِخ (an-náfiẖ), from Arabic نَافِخ (nāfiḵ).
From Andalusian Arabic مَنَاقِل (manáqil), from Arabic مِنْقَلَة (minqala, “bench”). Doublet of mancala.

Uncertain. Federico Corriente considers the Andalusian Arabic حَطْرَجْ (ḥaṭraj, “foolish”) that appears in Vocabulista in Arabico and that comes from the known root ه ت ر (h t r) (the same as مُهْتَر (muhtar, “disordered in his intellect”) in Lane’s lexicon).

parole.significato: the bush (remote, undeveloped area); the backcountry; the sticks; the middle of nowhere
parole.testo: Unknown. Proposed etymologies include: * From Andalusian Arabic [Term?]. * From Basque andur (“contemptible”). * From andar (“to walk”). First attested c. 1464-1474 (see quotations).
Borrowed from Andalusian Arabic, from Arabic أَفْيُون (ʔafyūn), ultimately from Ancient Greek ὄπιον (ópion). Doublet of opio.
From Andalusian Arabic لمط (lámṭ).

parole.significato: a drapery, tapestry; a patchwork hanging
parole.testo: From Andalusian Arabic الحنبل (al-ḥánbal), from Arabic حَنْبَل (ḥanbal, “ceremonial tapestry”). Doublet of alfombra and alhamar.
Borrowed from Andalusian Arabic الأَنْزِالْ (al-ʔanzél), from Arabic إِنْزَال (ʔinzāl), verbal noun of أَنْزَلَ (ʔanzala, “to get [something] down; to reveal”), having undergone imāla.
From Andalusian Arabic الرَبَض (ar-rabáḍ), from Arabic رَبَض (rabaḍ, “outskirts”). Cognate to Asturian, Portuguese arrabalde and Catalan raval.

parole.significato: earring (especially one that hangs down, as opposed to a stud)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Andalusian Arabic الرّقوة (arraqqáda, “that which sleeps constantly”).
Borrowed from Andalusian Arabic [Term?], from Arabic رطل (riṭl, raṭl). Doublet of litro.
Borrowed from Andalusian Arabic الرِيَاض (ar-riyáḍ), from Arabic رَوْضَة (rawḍa).
Borrowed from Andalusian Arabic الرُّبّ (ar-rúbb), from Arabic رُبّ (rubb).

parole.significato: rice (cereal plants, Oryza sativa of the grass family whose seeds are used as food)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Spanish arroz, borrowed from Andalusian Arabic روز (rawz), from Arabic *رَوْز (*rawz), from رُزّ (ruzz), borrowed from Ancient Greek ὄρυζα (óruza), from Proto-Iranian *wrinǰiš, from *wriHǰíš, from Proto-Indo-Iranian *wriHǰʰíš.

parole.significato: boss; chief (of Moors or other Arabic people)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Andalusian Arabic الرَّائِس (ar-ráyeç), from Arabic رَئِيس (raʔīs).
From Andalusian Arabic التَّقِيَّة (at-taqíah, “prevention”), ultimately from Arabic تقية (taqīyyah).

Borrowed from Andalusian Arabic الدار الصنعة (ad-dár aṣ-ṣánʕa), from دار الصناعة (dár aṣ-ṣináʕa), from Arabic دَار اَلصِّنَاعَة (dār aṣ-ṣināʕa, literally “house of industry”). Compare dársena and arsenal. Cognate to Catalan drassana.
Probably from Andalusian Arabic التشييع (at-tašyíʕ), from Arabic تَشْيِيع (tašyīʕ, “accompanying”)
Borrowed from Andalusian Arabic الطرقة (*aṭ-ṭarráqa), from Arabic مِطْرَقَة (miṭraqa).
Borrowed from Andalusian Arabic الطراحة (aṭ-ṭarráḥa).
Borrowed from Arabic تَابُوت (tābūt), via Andalusian Arabic. Compare Portuguese ataúde.
Borrowed from Andalusian Arabic الطوجة (aṭ-ṭáwča), from an Iberian substrate language.
Borrowed from Andalusian Arabic التُّوتِيَا (at-tutíyya), from Arabic تُوتِيَاء (tūtiyāʔ).

Inherited from Old Spanish atun, borrowed from Andalusian Arabic [Term?], from Arabic اَلتُّنّ (at-tunn, “tuna”), from Latin thunnus, from Ancient Greek θύννος (thúnnos). Compare Portuguese atum. See also the related tonina, which may have influenced this word.

parole.significato: jet (a form of compact, glistening coal, often used in jewelry)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Andalusian Arabic سبج (sabáj), from Arabic سَبَج (sabaj), borrowed from Middle Persian špk' (/⁠šabag⁠/), from šp (/⁠šab⁠/), from Old Persian 𐎧𐏁𐎱 (x-š-p /⁠xšapa⁠/), from Proto-Iranian *xšáfš, from Proto-Indo-Iranian *kšáps, from Proto-Indo-European *kʷséps.
Inherited from Old Spanish açafran, from Arabic زَعْفَرَان (zaʕfarān, “saffron”), via Andalusian Arabic.
From Andalusian Arabic, from Arabic الزَّهْرَة (az-zahra, “flower, blossom”); compare Italian zagara (“orange blossom”).
From Andalusian Arabic الزَّوْق (az-zawq, “the quicksilver”), from Arabic زَاؤُوق (zāʔūq, “quicksilver”).
Borrowed from Andalusian Arabic السطيح (as-suṭáyḥa), from Arabic سَطِيح (saṭīḥ, “flat, spread out”).
Borrowed from Arabic سَوْسَن (sawsan), via Andalusian Arabic. Cognate with Galician azucena and Portuguese açucena.

Inherited from Old Spanish azur, from an Andalusian Arabic *لَازُورْد (*lāzūrd), contracted form of Arabic لَازُوَرْد (lāzuward, “lapis lazuli”), from Persian لاجورد (lâjvard, “lapis lazuli”). Doublet of azur, from French. Cognate with English azure.
From Andalusian Arabic اَلزُّلَيْجَة (az-zuléyja), from Arabic اَلزُّلَيْج (az-zulayj, “polished stone”), formed as a diminutive of زُلُج (zuluj, “smooth rocks”).

parole.significato: an ancient measure of volume of liquids used in Castile, equivalent to 2.016 litres
parole.testo: Borrowed from Andalusian Arabic الثُّمُن (aṯ-ṯúmn), from Arabic ثُمُن (ṯumun), ثُمْن (ṯumn, “one eighth”). Doublet of tomín and celemín.

Inherited from Old Spanish açúcar, borrowed from Andalusian Arabic سكر (sukkar), from Arabic سُكَّر (sukkar), borrowed from Middle Persian 𐭱𐭪𐭥 (šakar), borrowed from Gandhari 𐨭𐨐𐨪 (śakara), from Sanskrit शर्क॑रा (śárkarā), from Proto-Indo-Aryan *śárkaraH, from Proto-Indo-Iranian *ćárkaraH, from Proto
Borrowed from Andalusian Arabic النزاهة (an-nazáha), from Arabic نزاهة (nazāha, “integrity, honesty”).
From Andalusian Arabic النَّقَّازَة (an-naqqáza), from Arabic نَقَّاز (naqqāz, “jumping bird”), from decoy birds that loosened themselves by jumping.
Borrowed from Arabic نِيل (nīl) via Andalusian Arabic, from Middle Persian 𐭭𐭩𐭫 (nyl /⁠nīl⁠/), ultimately from Sanskrit नील (nīla, “blue”).
From Old Spanish vatanna, from Andalusian Arabic [script needed] (baṭána), from Arabic بِطَانَة (biṭāna, “inside, lining, liner”).

parole.significato: dumb, having the properties of an imbecile
parole.testo: Borrowed from Andalusian Arabic بَرْدِلَاقَس (berdilāqaš, “common purslane”), from Latin portulāca. Doublet of verdolaga.

parole.significato: trivial, banal, of no importance, meaningless
parole.testo: Borrowed from Andalusian Arabic, from Arabic بَلَدِيّ (baladiyy).

parole.significato: a cheap and worthless thing; a trinket, trifle
parole.testo: From Andalusian Arabic [script needed] (báṭ[i]la), itself from Arabic بَاطِلَة (bāṭila, “vain, useless”).
From balde (“in vain”) + -ar, from Andalusian Arabic بَاطِل (báṭil), ultimately from Arabic بَاطِل (bāṭil, “invalid, null, futile”).
From balda (“(obsolete) worthless thing”) + -ío, from Andalusian Arabic [script needed] (báṭ[i]la), itself from Arabic بَاطِلَة (bāṭila, “vain, useless”).

Borrowed from Andalusian Arabic بَرِّيّ (barriyy, “exterior”), referring to the outer, surrounding or less civilized or urbanized parts of a city, from classical Arabic بَرِّيّ (barriyy, “wild”). Compare Portuguese bairro, Catalan barri.
Probably from Andalusian Arabic بَاطَان (bāṭān), from Arabic بِطَانَة (biṭāna, “liner, lining”).
Borrowed from Andalusian Arabic, from Arabic بَلُّوطَة (ballūṭa, “oak, acorn”), from Syriac ܒܠܘܛܐ.

Inherited from Old Spanish, borrowed from Andalusian Arabic بِسْنَاج (bisnāj), بِسْتِنَاجَة (bistināja), بِشْتِْنَاجَة (bištināja), بِشْتِنَاقَة (bištināqa, “parsnip”), from Latin pastināca (“parsnip, carrot”).

parole.significato: cahiz (a traditional unit of dry measure equivalent to about 665.8 liters)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Spanish cafiz, from Andalusian Arabic, from Arabic قَفِيز (qafīz). Cognate with Ancient Greek καπίθη (kapíthē), Catalan cahís, and Galician and Portuguese cacifo.
From Andalusian Arabic قلفط (qalafaṭa, qalafaṭe, “to caulk”). Compare Libyan Arabic قلفاط, Maltese qalfat, and etymology 2 in Arabic قالة (qāla).
From Andalusian Arabic كَنْبِنْيَا (*kanpinyā), from Late Latin campānia, which also entered directly from Late Latin as campaña.
Borrowed from Andalusian Arabic قِرْمِز (qirmiz).

parole.significato: ceviche (raw seafood cured by marination in an acidic medium such as citrus, vinegar, or other souring agent, found pri…
parole.testo: Uncertain. Theories include: * from cebo + -iche * from Andalusian Arabic [Term?], from Arabic سِكْبَاج m (sikbāj), سِكْبَاجَة f (sikbāja, “the dish sikbaj, meat cooked in vinegar”), from Middle Persian *sḵbʾk' (*sikbāg) (whence Persian سکبا (sekbâ)), in which case cebiche is cognate to Portuguese e

parole.significato: mint (where coins or money are made)
parole.testo: From Andalusian Arabic سَكَّة (sakka), from Arabic سِكَّة (sikka).

parole.significato: celemin (a traditional unit of dry measure equivalent to about 4.6 liters)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Andalusian Arabic, from Arabic ثُمُنِ (ṯumuni, “of one-eighth”). Doublet of tomín and azumbre. Cognate with Portuguese celamim and Galician celamín.
Borrowed from Andalusian Arabic, from Arabic سِتَارَة (sitāra).
From Andalusian Arabic, from Arabic كَهْرَبَاء (kahrabāʔ).
Ultimately from Andalusian Arabic بَاطِل (báṭil), from Arabic بَاطِل (bāṭil, “vain”)

parole.significato: escabeche (a dish of fried fish, or other food, marinated in vinegar)
parole.testo: From Andalusian Arabic اَلسُّكَّبَاج (as-sukkabáj), from Arabic اَلسِّكْبَاجَة (as-sikbāja), feminine of سِكْبَاج (sikbāj), from Middle Persian [script needed] (*sḵbʾk' /⁠*sikbāg⁠/) (whence Persian سکبا (sekbâ)). Cf. cebiche.
Borrowed from Andalusian Arabic إشْكِرْلاطَ (ʔiškirlāṭa), from Arabic سِقِلّاط (siqillāṭ), from Byzantine Greek σιγιλλᾶτος (sigillâtos), from Latin textum sigillātum (literally “sealed text”).
Borrowed from Andalusian Arabic خَلَّابَة (ḵallāba).

parole.significato: English or American bushel (a dry measure)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Andalusian Arabic فَنِيقَة (faníqa), from Arabic فَنِيقَة (fanīqa).

parole.significato: a sweet treat with a twisted, spiral form, primarily made from flour, eggs, and either sugar or honey.
parole.testo: Possibly of Andalusian Arabic origin. First attested in 1874.
From Andalusian Arabic جلبان (“grasspea”)

Possibly from garfa (“animal's claw”), from Andalusian Arabic جَارْفَا (gárfa, “handful”), from Arabic غُرْفَة (ḡurfa, “cup or dipper”), from غَرَفَ (ḡarafa, “to ladle”), with influence from garfio (“hook”). Or, possibly from Vulgar Latin *garra, from Gaulish *garrā (“leg”) (compare Breton gar, Old

parole.significato: an arch or similar structure used to determine the clearance of a moving vehicle (in a drive-through, a railway station…
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Spanish [Term?], from Andalusian Arabic قَالِب (qálib), from Arabic قَالَب (qālab), قَالِب (qālib, “form, mold”), from Ancient Greek κᾱλοπόδιον (kālopódion, “shoemaker's last”). Doublet of calibre.

parole.significato: a type of flatbread common in Chile and Bolivia
parole.testo: Borrowed from Andalusian Arabic حَلُّون (ḥallūn).

According to the Royal Spanish Academy, most likely derived from Andalusian Arabic كان خرا (ḵrā kān), meaning "it was shit". An alternative theory is a borrowing from Old High German arag, arg (“worthless, lazy, bad”) or Gothic *𐌰𐍂𐌲𐍃 (*args), both from Proto-Germanic *argaz, whence also Old English

parole.significato: charcoal made from the stones of pressed olives
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Spanish, from Andalusian Arabic الرَاهْج (ar-rāhj).

parole.significato: a type of short cape without a hood (capilla or capucha)
parole.testo: From older ferrehuelo, perhaps from Andalusian Arabic فرويل (occurring in an inventory constituted in the year 1161, Toledo; Coromines vocalizes it as fariwîl), folk-etymologized into herrero (“blacksmith”) + -uelo (diminutive ending). Coromines appears confident in this interpretation of the Arabic
Borrowed from Andalusian Arabic, from Arabic كَسْلَان (kaslān, “lazy”), and influenced by holgar. Compare Galician lacazán.

parole.significato: A type of flute intended to imitate the sound of an organ; used predominantly by Moriscos in medieval Spain.
parole.testo: Aphaeresis of ajabeba, from Old Spanish axabeba, from Andalusian Arabic الشَّبَّابَة (aš-šabbába), from Arabic شَبَّابَة (šabbāba).
Borrowed from Andalusian Arabic شَبّ (šább), from Classical Arabic شَبّ (šabb, “alum”).
From Andalusian Arabic الشِّنَاب (*aš-šináb), from Arabic صِنَاب (ṣināb).
Inherited from Old Spanish xeque, borrowed from Andalusian Arabic شَيْخ, from Arabic شيخ.
Borrowed from Andalusian Arabic [Term?], from Arabic شَرِيف (šarīf).

parole.significato: horseman, horsewoman, rider (someone who rides a horse)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Spanish ginete, borrowed from Andalusian Arabic زَنَاتِي (zanáti), the Zenati or Zenata Berbers, known as excellent horse breeders. Cognate with Galician xinete and Portuguese ginete.
Variant of aljofaina, from Andalusian Arabic اَلْجُفَيْنَة (al-juféyna), from Arabic جُفَيْنَة (jufayna), diminutive of جَفْنَة (jafna).
Borrowed from Andalusian Arabic هَضُبَّة (haḍóbba), from Classical Arabic هَضَبَة (haḍaba).
Augmentative of juba, variant of aljuba, from Andalusian Arabic الجُبَّة (al-júbba), from Classical Arabic جُبَّة (jubba).

parole.significato: jack mackerel (edible fish of the genus Caranx or Trachurus)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Spanish [Term?], from Andalusian Arabic شُورِيل (šuríl), from Latin saurus, from Ancient Greek σαῦρος (saûros, “lizard”).
Borrowed from Andalusian Arabic لِيمَة (līma), from Arabic لَيْمُون (laymūn, “lemon, lime”).

From the earlier momarrache under the influence of mamar, itself from the earlier moharrache under the influence of momo (“funny face”), borrowed from Andalusian Arabic مهرج, ultimately from Arabic مُهَرِّج (muharrij).

parole.significato: of, from or relating to La Mancha
parole.testo: From Andalusian Arabic المنشا (al Mansha); Mancha + -ego.

parole.significato: maquila, half-almud (a traditional unit of dry measure of variable size)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Andalusian Arabic مَكِيلَة (makíla), from Arabic مَكِيلَة (makīla, “measured”). In reference to factories, via clipping of maquiladora, from maquilar (“to assemble”) + -adora (“-ator: forming agent nouns”), from maquilar's original sense of taking a toll of grain.
Inherited from Old Spanish [Term?], from Andalusian Arabic مرباط (marbáṭ, “bag on the belt”), from Arabic مِرْبَط (mirbaṭ, “rope, hawser”).
Borrowed from Andalusian Arabic مرشم (máršam), possibly from Arabic رَسَمَ (rasama, “draw, trace”).

parole.significato: a type of closely-fitted Moorish robe similar to a smock frock
parole.testo: From Andalusian Arabic mallúṭa, from Arabic [script needed] (mallūṭah), from Ancient Greek χλᾰμῠ́ς (khlămŭ́s, “cloak, robe”).
Borrowed from Andalusian Arabic مَبْرُومَة (mabrúm(a)), from Arabic مَبْرُومَة (mabrūma).

parole.significato: marzipan (confection made with almond paste, or another nut such as peanut)
parole.testo: Two possible theories: * From Old Spanish [Term?], from Andalusian Arabic بسمة, from Ancient Greek παξαμάδιον (paxamádion, “cookie”), with influence from masa (“mass”) and pan (“bread”). * From Italian marzapane, thought to be derived from Arabic مَرْطَبَان (marṭabān, “spice box”), from Martaban (မု

parole.significato: mane (longer hair growth around head of male lions)
parole.testo: From Andalusian Arabic مُلَيِّنَة, from classical Arabic مُلَيِّنَة (mulayyina, “softening”).
Inherited from Old Spanish [Term?], from Andalusian Arabic مُغَطّة (muḡáṭṭa), from the Arabic root غ ط و (ḡ ṭ w, “to cover, to wrap”).
Borrowed from Andalusian Arabic مُهِين (muhīn), from Arabic مَهِين (mahīn).
Inherited from Old Spanish [Term?], from Andalusian Arabic ميدان (méydan), from Arabic مَيْدَان (maydān, “field, arena, open tract”).
From a variant *násqa in Andalusian Arabic of Arabic نَسَق (nasaq).

Borrowed from Andalusian Arabic بَّطّ (paṭṭ), from Arabic بَطّ (baṭṭ, “duck”), from Persian بَت (bat, “duck”). Sense of "homosexual" may be related to the Ancient Greek πάθος (páthos, “to suffer, to be passive”).
Borrowed from Andalusian Arabic رباط (ribāt).
Inherited from Old Spanish requa, from Andalusian Arabic رَكْبَة (rakba), from Arabic رَكَبَة (rakaba), plural of رَاكِب (rākib, “rider”).
Borrowed from Andalusian Arabic [Term?], from Arabic رَسَن (rasan).
From Andalusian Arabic رخ (ruḵḵ), from Arabic رُخّ (ruḵḵ).
From Andalusian Arabic رَابِطَة (rābiṭa), from Arabic رِبَاط (ribāṭ).

Borrowed from Andalusian Arabic *شُپَيْپَة (šopáypa, šupáypa), diminutive of Andalusian Arabic شَپَّاپَة (šappā́pa), from Mozarabic *supa (“chunk of bread soaked in oil”) from Late Latin suppa, from Proto-Germanic *suppǭ f (“soup, broth”) or *supô m (“soup, broth”).
From Andalusian Arabic طَبَق (ṭabáq), from Arabic طَبَق (ṭabaq, “plate”).
Borrowed from Andalusian Arabic تَشْبِيك (tašbík), from Arabic تَشْبِيك (tašbīk).
Possibly from Andalusian Arabic [script needed] (mata ḥínna, “dyed with henna”).

parole.significato: mill for crushing flour powered by horses
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Spanish atahona, borrowed from Andalusian Arabic, from Arabic طَاحُونَة (ṭāḥūna).

parole.significato: a slim bag made of linen cloth
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Spanish talega, from Andalusian Arabic تَعْلِيقَة (taʕlīqa, “something hung, suspended”), akin to Galician taleiga.
Borrowed from Andalusian Arabic تابول (ṭabbūl), hypocorism/diminutive of Arabic طُنْبُور (ṭunbūr); see Persian طبل (“drum”).
Borrowed from Andalusian Arabic تَرَصِيَّعْ (taraçéaʕ), from Arabic تَرْصِيع (tarṣīʕ, “putting together, incrustation”).
From the earlier form tarahe, from Andalusian Arabic, from Arabic طَرْفَاء (ṭarfāʔ, “tamarisk”).

parole.significato: fare (money paid for a transport ticket)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Spanish [Term?], from Andalusian Arabic [Term?], from Classical Arabic تَعْرِفَة (taʕrifa).
Borrowed from Andalusian Arabic طارمة (ṭārima), from Arabic طَارِمَة (ṭārima).

Borrowed from Andalusian Arabic تاقرة (tāqra, “milking pail”), which is also found as a liquid measure tagra rarely in Galician-Portuguese, in Old Spanish tagara (“bowl”) and Old Leonese tagara, tagarra (“bowl”), and in Spanish tarreñas, tarrañuelas (“two pieces of slate or earthenware placed betwee

Inherited from Old Spanish taça, from Andalusian Arabic طَاس, from Arabic طَاس (ṭās), from Middle Persian tšt' (tašt); see there for more information. More at tejer, tela, telera, and tecno, which all may come from the same Indo-European root.

parole.significato: tomin (a traditional unit of mass equivalent to about 0.6 g)
parole.testo: From Andalusian Arabic ثُمْن (ṯúmn), from Arabic ثُمْن (ṯumn, “one-eighth”), from the root ن (n) م (m) ث (ṯ-m-n). Originally used in reference to it forming one-eighth of a castellano. Doublet of azumbre and celemín.
From Andalusian Arabic وزير (wazír), from Arabic وَزِير (wazīr, “minister”). Compare alguacil.
From Andalusian Arabic زَاح ([a]záḥ), from Arabic أَزَاحَ (ʔazāḥa, “to remove; to move to another place”).

parole.significato: rear (back part of someone or something)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Andalusian Arabic صَٰقَا (çáqā), from Arabic صَقَا (ṣaqā, “rear”).

parole.significato: swain, boy, lad, youth, young man
parole.testo: From Andalusian Arabic زغال (zaḡál, “young; brave”), from Arabic زُغْلُول (zuḡlūl).

Though the Andalusian Arabic is unattested, this Castilian form exposes typical Andalusian Spanish developments, avowing itself to be from a variant of Arabic سُوَيْدَاء (suwaydāʔ) as well as synonymously used Catalan sosa whence sosa and Italian soda whence soda.

parole.significato: vestibule; front hall or entryway; foyer
parole.testo: From Andalusian Arabic إِسْطِوَان (ʔisṭiwān), from Arabic أُسْطُوَانَة (ʔusṭuwāna, “pillar”).
From Andalusian Arabic سَخِينَة (saḵīna), from Arabic سَخِينَة (saḵīna).
From Andalusian Arabic زَهِيم (zahīm, “unpleasant”), from Arabic زَهِم (zahim, “greasy, filthy, fetid”).
From Andalusian Arabic السلام عليكم (as-salám ʕalík), from Arabic السَّلَامُ عَلَيْكُم (as-salāmu ʕalaykum, “peace be with you; hello”).
From obsolete zalama, from Andalusian Arabic السلام عليكم (as-salám ʕalík), from Arabic السَّلَامُ عَلَيْكُم (as-salāmu ʕalaykum, “peace be with you; hello”).
From Andalusian Arabic السَّلِامْ عَلِيكُمْ (aç-çalém ʕalícum), from Arabic السَّلَامُ عَلَيْكُمْ (as-salām ʕalaīkum); "peace be with you", "hello".

Inherited from Old Spanish çanahoria, from Andalusian Arabic *سَفُنَّارْيَة (*safunnārya), from Arabic إِسْفَنَارِيَّة (ʔisfanāriyya) (compare Libyan Arabic سفنّاريّة (sfənnāriyya) and Maltese zunnarija), from Ancient Greek σταφυλίνη ἀγρία (staphulínē agría, “wild carrot”). Cognate to Asturian zanah
Borrowed from Andalusian Arabic سَرَنْد (“sarand”), from Persian سَرَنْد (sarand, “sieve”).
Inherited from Old Spanish [Term?], from Andalusian Arabic زورزال (zurzál), from Classical Arabic زُرْزُور (zurzūr, “thrush”).
Variant of sulla, from Andalusian Arabic سُلَّة (sulla), سِلَّة (silla), meaning this very plant.
Inherited from Old Spanish çumo, from Andalusian Arabic, from Arabic زُوم (zūm, “juice, sap”), from Ancient Greek ζωμός (zōmós).
Borrowed from Andalusian Arabic, from Arabic الْقِلْي (al-qily).

parole.significato: amber (of a brownish yellow colour, like that of most amber.)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Spanish ambar, borrowed from Andalusian Arabic [script needed] (ʕánbar), from Arabic عَنْبَر (ʕanbar, “ambergris”).

Either inherited from Latin apage (“go away”), from Ancient Greek άπαγε (ápage), or alternatively borrowed from Arabic اِبْعَد (ibʕad, dialectally also abʕad), imperative of بَعِدَ (baʕida, “to go away”), via Andalusian Arabic. As both words have the same meaning and could both easily have yielded S

parole.significato: crazy, insane, mad, nuts (asserting that something is out of place in the head)
parole.testo: Uncertain. Inherited from Old Spanish loco, perhaps from Andalusian Arabic لَوْقَاء (láwqa), from Arabic لَوْقَاء (lawqāʔ), feminine singular form of أَلْوَق (ʔalwaq, “stupid”), by reinterpreting the final Andalusian Arabic -a as the Ibero-Romance -a and back-forming the masculine with -o. Edward Ro
